{"decision":"Anthony's word, 2026-07-30, after asking for the open requirements to be strongly scrutinised: an unaccepted requirement that is not value-adding and only causes confusion should be retired as "considered, but not accepted" rather than carried. Ten of twenty-six went. All are `dropped`, not deleted: the capture was real and the reasoning is worth keeping, so each keeps its full statement and a snapshot of its final state on the timeline (`epoch:prune-proposed`).

DROPPED AS NOT VALUE-ADDING (7).

`req:drift-rolls-up-to-a-score` and `req:framework-is-chosen-not-defaulted` — both record a DOUBT rather than a need, and say so in their own names: "probably NOT from a single scalar" and "a framework registry is probably the wrong fix". A requirement that argues against its own mechanism is a Decision wearing the wrong hat. The live fact inside the second (`Project.domain` is written and never read) survives inside `req:defaults-do-not-assert`.

`req:friction-has-a-baseline` and `req:friction-has-a-severity-bar` — measuring reflow2's own usability against a baseline, and a threshold at which friction becomes scheduled work. Both are backlog hygiene dressed as product requirements: the answer to unconverted friction reports is to act on them, not to model them. The severity-bar one carries real evidence (eight brainmaker items unconverted) and that evidence belongs in the backlog, which is where it now lives.

`req:context-is-a-modelled-quantity` — `cap:bounded-reads` already answers the acute version, where a read that would not fit says so and names what it withheld. What remained was design-time estimation, which the requirement's own text calls the weak half.

`req:blocking-is-partial` — freezing drifted work while the rest proceeds. Nobody has been hurt by the all-or-nothing gate; speculative.

`req:adopt-says-how-much-it-got` — REDUNDANT. "Adopt reports how much was recovered" restates `req:coverage-visible`, which is accepted and delivered by `cap:coverage` ("say what the design has never heard of"). Two requirements for one need is the confusion this pass was called to remove.

FOLDED INTO `req:defaults-do-not-assert` (3). `req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert`, `req:functional-vocabulary-computes` and `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` are one rule stated four times — node defaults, edge defaults, declared-but-unread vocabulary, and detector-ignored properties are the same defect: THE SCHEMA MUST NOT DECLARE WHAT NOTHING READS OR CHECKS. Their specific evidence is preserved inside the surviving requirement rather than lost with them. `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` had exactly ONE edge, so it was already an orphan in all but name.

NOT TOUCHED, and worth recording why. The 2026-07-28 planning cluster — `req:epochs-can-be-planned`, `req:plans-move-honestly`, `req:version-combination-is-an-object`, `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` — are Anthony's own ideas, quoting him directly (the Black-Scholes analogy for plan volatility, "in systems engineering, I think this would be 2 views of the same system"). They are structurally disconnected, but that means CAPTURED AND NEVER WIRED, not low value: disconnection is a fact about edges, not about worth, and treating it as a proxy would have pruned exactly the wrong four. The fix for those is to wire them, not to retire them. `req:assumptions-are-first-class` (ordinary risk practice) and `req:correspondence-rules-are-stateable` (ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010) likewise stand: standard architecture-description ground for a user who works in UAF/DoDAF.","name":"Ten proposed requirements considered and not accepted — seven dropped, three folded into one rule","rationale":"The prompt for this was his: "if some of them are not value added and just cause confusion, then we don't have to do them — we can retire them as considered, but not accepted."

The test applied to each was whether the requirement would change what anyone BUILDS. A requirement that records a doubt does not; it records that a mechanism looked wrong, which is a Decision. A requirement that restates one already accepted does not; it splits one thread in two. A requirement that describes how the project should manage itself does not; it is process. What survived is everything with a code citation, a real incident, or a standing external practice behind it.

Two independent signals agreed on four of the ten, which is why the structural check was worth running before deciding rather than after: `req:framework-is-chosen-not-defaulted`, `req:functional-vocabulary-computes`, `req:friction-has-a-baseline` and `req:friction-has-a-severity-bar` were each sitting in a `disconnected_community` island AND on the retire list on their merits. But the same check listed four of Anthony's own ideas as islands too, so agreement between the signals was evidence and never the criterion.

DROPPED, NOT DELETED, and the distinction is the retire-from-design skill's central one. These were genuinely considered — several were found by measurement, and one (`req:supporting-is-not-conflict`) was found by using the graph in anger. Deleting them would erase why the surviving rules are shaped as they are, and would let the same captures be re-made next quarter by someone who could not see they had been weighed. `dropped` also stops them raising `unsatisfied_requirement`, so the open list means what it says again.","status":"accepted"}
